analysis.one_liner: Imposes safety rules on freight trains carrying hazardous materials, including two-person crews and trackside defect detectors.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a bipartisan pair with 17 cosponsors split evenly between parties, never received a committee markup or a floor vote in the House and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a year in which toxic train derailments drew national attention, this bill would have required railroads to tell state and tribal emergency officials what hazardous materials are moving through their communities, install hotbox defect detectors every 10 miles on routes carrying hazardous cargo, and run most such trains with at least a two-person crew. It would also have mandated minimum inspection time for rail cars, cut 10 times larger fines for safety violations, retired older, crash-prone tank cars by May 2025, and charged each large railroad a $1 million annual fee to fund training for local firefighters and first responders.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work along freight rail routes, where hazardous materials pass through their towns every day; local firefighters and emergency crews who would get more advance information and better training; rail car inspectors and train crews whose work standards would be set in federal law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities along freight rail lines and first responders

how_it_helps.text: Requires shippers and rail carriers to give state and tribal emergency response commissioners advance notice of hazardous materials moving through their jurisdictions, plus a written gas discharge plan [S3].

Directs the Transportation Department to require hotbox detectors — trackside sensors that catch overheating wheel bearings before they fail — along every 10-mile segment of track used by hazardous-materials trains, and to set rules for how railroads must respond to detector alerts [S3].
Writes a two-person crew minimum into law for freight trains, with no exceptions for trains carrying toxic-by-inhalation cargo, long strings of flammable tank cars, or trains over 7,500 feet [S3].
Raises maximum civil penalties roughly tenfold, to the greater of $750,000–$1.75 million or a percentage of the violator's annual income, for safety violations involving hazardous materials [S3].

Forces the retirement of older DOT-111 tank cars for flammable liquids by May 1, 2025 — four years sooner than current law — and sets minimum inspection time requirements for qualified mechanical inspectors [S2, S3].
Charges each Class I railroad a $1 million annual fee and expands grant funding to $4 million per year to train local emergency responders on hazardous materials [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The large Class I freight railroads and, in part, their customers: they would bear the cost of detectors, crews, inspections, tank-car replacements, higher fines, and the new $1 million annual fee, some of which would likely show up in freight rates passed to shippers and consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Class I freight railroads and freight customers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are substantial: hotbox detectors every 10 miles, mandatory two-person crews, faster tank-car retirement, and inspection requirements all add operating expense for railroads, and some of that cost would be passed to shippers and eventually to prices for goods moved by rail [S2, S3].

The bill includes significant carve-outs: the crew-size mandate does not apply to low-speed, small-revenue railroads, yard tracks, and certain short moves, and railroads could seek waivers, so coverage is not universal [S3].

Critics of crew-size and fixed-spacing detector mandates argued that safety rules should be based on demonstrated risk and performance rather than fixed headcounts and mileages, and that the 2025 DOT-111 phase-out deadline was aggressive for the available fleet — the bill sets numbers without a formal risk analysis [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill targets a real, documented failure mode — derailments of hazardous-materials trains that devastate towns and overwhelm local emergency crews — and shifts the cost of preventing them onto the companies that profit from hauling the cargo. The costs to the rail industry are real and would partly reach consumers through freight rates, but they are modest next to the cleanup, health, and evacuation costs of a single major derailment, which today fall largely on the towns involved. The main design weaknesses are the exceptions and waivers in the crew mandate and the aggressive tank-car deadline.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to the Railroads Subcommittee, where it sat with no markup, no vote, and no floor action before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Christopher Deluzio, a Pennsylvania Democrat, and Representative Nick LaLota, a New York Republican, introduced the bill together on March 21, 2023 [S1, S3].

It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Science, Space, and Technology Committee, and the next day to the Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee [S1, S5].
No further action was recorded: no subcommittee vote, no full committee markup, no floor vote, in the roughly 21 months remaining in the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large Class I freight railroads came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, they avoided a two-person crew mandate, a hotbox detector every 10 miles, tenfold higher fines, mandatory inspector time minimums, an accelerated tank-car retirement, and the $1 million annual fee. Communities along rail lines and local emergency responders gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large freight railroads avoided new safety mandates

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 9 of 224 Republicans and 8 of 216 Democrats — but because the bill never reached a vote, party positions on the substance were never tested on the floor.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed two-person crews, a hotbox detector every 10 miles on hazmat routes, inspection minimums, tenfold higher fines, an accelerated tank-car retirement, and a $1 million annual fee per carrier. The industry's interest lay in avoiding these costs, which would otherwise have come out of its operating margins.

Shippers would face new advance-notification duties for hazardous cargo, and higher railroad compliance costs would likely reach them through freight rates — though a prevented derailment that closes their routes or destroys their cargo is a cost they already bear under the status quo.
Forcing older DOT-111 cars off the rails for flammable liquids by May 2025 and funding new tank car research creates demand for safer DOT-117-compliant cars and equipment.
A mandate to install hotbox detectors every 10 miles on hazardous-materials routes, plus $22 million in research funding, creates a market for trackside detection technology.
